standard.title: Prime Factorisation and Exponent Notation
standard.description: represent natural numbers as products of powers of prime numbers using exponent notation
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify prime and composite numbers and know their basic properties (from AC9M6N02). Students can use factor trees to find factors of numbers.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students represent any natural number as a product of powers of prime factors using exponent notation, and apply this to find lowest common multiples and greatest common divisors.

nodes.label: Exponent notation for repeated multiplication
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students understand exponent notation as shorthand for repeated multiplication and can convert between expanded and exponent forms.
nodes.minimum_width: Write 2×2×2×2 as 2⁴ and vice versa for small bases and exponents.
nodes.typical_width: Convert fluently between repeated multiplication and exponent notation for bases 2, 3, 5, 7 and small exponents; state what the base and exponent each mean.
wider: Investigate the sequence 2¹, 2², 2³, ... and connect to powers of 2 in computing contexts (bytes, storage).
Explore 10¹, 10², 10³ and connect to place value notation (links to AC9M7N03).

response_modes.reason: Exponent notation is a new symbolic system. Students need fluency reading and writing it before applying it to prime factorisation.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot fluently read and write exponent notation cannot record or interpret prime factorisation results in Node 2 — the symbolic system is the medium for all subsequent work in this standard.
success_criteria: Correctly converts between repeated multiplication and exponent notation.
States the meaning of the base and exponent in a given expression.
Does not confuse aⁿ with a×n (e.g. does not evaluate 2³ as 6).

nodes.label: Prime factorisation via factor trees
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can express any natural number as a product of prime factors using a factor tree, and write the result using exponent notation.
nodes.minimum_width: Use a factor tree to find the prime factorisation of a given composite number (e.g. 36 = 2² × 3²).
nodes.typical_width: Find prime factorisations for a range of composite numbers including larger ones (e.g. 360), write results in exponent notation, and verify by expanding.
wider: Show that different factor trees for the same number always yield the same prime factorisation (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic — informally).
Investigate which numbers have only one prime factor (powers of primes) and what their factor trees look like.

response_modes.reason: Students often believe different factor trees can produce different prime factorisations. Seeing multiple paths to the same result across several numbers resolves this misconception.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who believe prime factorisation is non-unique cannot apply the LCM/GCD algorithm in Node 3 correctly — the entire method depends on there being one canonical factorisation to compare.
success_criteria: Produces a correct factor tree and writes the result in exponent notation.
Verifies the factorisation by expanding and multiplying.
Understands that the prime factorisation of a number is unique.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The uniqueness of prime factorisation (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, informally) is a rich structural insight — advancing students who explore multiple factor trees and observe convergence are engaging with a deep number theory idea.

nodes.label: LCM and GCD from prime factorisations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students use prime factorisations to find the lowest common multiple and greatest common divisor of pairs of natural numbers.
nodes.minimum_width: Find the LCM and GCD of two numbers using their prime factorisations.
nodes.typical_width: Apply the LCM and GCD in context: e.g. find when two cyclic events coincide (LCM), or find the largest equal shares (GCD).
wider: Explore the relationship LCM(a,b) × GCD(a,b) = a × b and verify for several pairs.
Apply LCM to scheduling problems: if two buses leave every 12 and 18 minutes, when do they next leave together?

response_modes.reason: The algorithm (take highest power of each prime for LCM; lowest power for GCD) requires an explicit systematic scaffold. Students who proceed by listing multiples/factors miss the prime factorisation connection.
LCM and GCD require coordinating prime factorisation, exponent comparison, and contextual interpretation simultaneously.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot apply the systematic LCM/GCD algorithm from prime factorisations revert to listing methods — this blocks the connection to AC9M7N04 fraction simplification and AC9M7N06 common denominator work where the prime factorisation method is the efficient path.
success_criteria: Correctly finds LCM and GCD for a given pair using prime factorisations.
Can explain why the method works (not just apply it).
Applies LCM or GCD appropriately when presented with a contextual problem.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The relationship LCM × GCD = a × b and its application to scheduling problems offers advancing students genuine algebraic-structural reasoning within the Year 7 band.
